sentences: Credit utilization is the most important driver of default risk, with a strong effect: risk increases as the share of the credit limit in use rises, and the rise is concentrated above about 0.72.
The number of past delinquencies is the second or third most important driver, with a moderate to strong effect, and risk jumps once an applicant has at least one delinquency.
Credit utilization matters more than the number of past delinquencies.
Income is also among the top three drivers, with a moderate to strong effect: risk decreases as income rises, and income matters more than the length of credit history.
The data do not settle whether credit utilization and the number of past delinquencies interact, although the effect of delinquencies appears somewhat larger at high utilization.
The length of credit history has at most a moderate effect, with risk decreasing as history gets longer, and it ranks roughly fourth to sixth in importance.
The debt-to-income ratio has at most a moderate effect on default risk and ranks fourth to eighth, with no clear movement resolved at this sample size.
Recent credit inquiries, age, months at the current address and the number of dependents hardly matter for default risk.
